transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You found the friction force correctly. Can you think of another way to check if this answer makes sense?
Um, I don't know. How would I check it?
You can check by estimating the normal force and seeing if the friction force seems reasonable for that.
The normal force is just mg, so 49. Times 0.2 is 9.8. I don't really get what else to check.
You're on the right track, but the normal force isn't just mg here. What's the component of gravity perpendicular to the incline?
Wait, isn't normal force always equal to the weight? I don't understand the perpendicular thing.
No, the normal force isn't always equal to the weight. On an incline, only part of the weight pushes straight into the surface. Can you picture the block on the slope?
Yeah I can picture it. But I still don't know how to get the part that pushes into the slope.
Got it. Give me a second.
The part that pushes into the slope is mg times cos(30°). Try calculating that.
Okay, 49 times cos 30 is about 42.4. So friction is 0.2 times 42.4, which is 8.5 newtons?
Yes, that's right! You found the normal force and then the friction force correctly. Good job!
Cool, so on a slope N is mg cos 30, not mg. I'll fix my first line. Thanks.
